paragraphs.context: The potentials studied in this book are seldom differentiable. On $\mathbb R^2$, for instance, the function $\log |x|$ tends to $-\infty $ at the origin, yet its Laplacian has a precise meaning: it is $2\pi $ times the Dirac mass at the origin (proposition 2.2.1 ). The derivatives obtained in this way are distributions. For subharmonic functions, and later for plurisubharmonic ones, the relevant second derivatives are positive distributions, and a positive distribution is a measure. The measure attached to a potential records where its mass lies, including the mass concentrated at its singularities; measures and distributions are therefore the basic language of potential theory.

paragraphs.context: Let $X$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold, and let $T$ be a closed positive $(1,1)$-current on $X$. By theorem 7.3.2 , every point of $X$ has a coordinate neighborhood on which $T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ with $u$ plurisubharmonic. On the overlap of two such neighborhoods the two local potentials differ by a pluriharmonic function, and in general no choice of the local potentials makes them agree. For instance, let $X$ have positive dimension and let $T=\omega $ be a Kähler form. A global potential $u$ would be plurisubharmonic on $X$, so it would attain its maximum, being upper semicontinuous on the compact space $X$. The set where it does so is closed, and it is also open by the maximum principle (proposition 3.1.4 ), applied on coordinate balls, where $u$ is subharmonic (theorem 8.2.1 ). Thus $u$ would be constant and $\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=0$. The obstruction is the cohomology class of $T$: by the $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-lemma (theorem 14.1.7 ), if $\theta $ is a smooth closed form in the class of $T$, then $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ for a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\varphi $ on $X$, unique up to an additive constant. We prove this by solving a Laplace equation for the trace of $T$, after developing the elliptic theory that this requires from the beginning; the same argument shows that the real $(1,1)$-cohomology of $X$ is finite dimensional. Closed positive currents in the class of $\theta $ therefore correspond, up to additive constants, to the functions in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ (definition 13.1.3 ), and the rest of the book works with such potentials.
